result: Current low-magnification objectives have low numerical aperture (0.1-0.2) and poor depth resolution (tens of microns), making them unsuitable for confocal and nonlinear microscopy of thick specimens like mouse embryos.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C4, C6, C8, and C15 establish the limitations of existing low-magnification objectives through both general knowledge and specific measurements (Table 1 showing 38-51 µm axial resolution for 5x/0.15 N.A. lens). These claims are well-supported by cited literature and comparative data.

result: The Mesolens avoids stitching artifacts (checkerboard patterns, registration errors) that plague tiled imaging approaches by capturing the entire field in a single scan.
evaluation: Claims C9-C11 and C73 describe known problems with stitching (supported by citation to Legesse et al., 2015) and contrast this with the Mesolens' continuous scanning approach. The advantage is logically sound and demonstrated in the imaging data.

result: The Mesolens was designed with 4x magnification and N.A. ~0.5 based on optical principles showing that below N.A. 0.45, axial resolution becomes insufficient for sub-cellular imaging.
evaluation: Claims C14, C43-C47 describe the design rationale based on established optical equations (Equations 1-2) and calculations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The design specifications are well-justified by optical theory.

result: The Mesolens has specifications of 4x magnification, N.A. 0.47, working distances of 3.15-3.74 mm for different immersion media, <0.7% distortion, full visible range color correction, and <3 µm field flatness.
evaluation: Claims C77-C84 present the design specifications of the Mesolens. These are stated specifications supported by measurements (C105 confirms field flatness) and demonstrated performance (C121 shows chromatic correction).

result: The Mesolens was designed using Zemax software with 15-17 optical elements up to 63 mm diameter, incorporating adjustable correction rings, compensator plates, and chromatic reflectors for multi-immersion capability.
evaluation: Claims C43, C51-C60 describe the design and construction methodology. These are factual descriptions of the instrument construction supported by Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing spot diagrams.

result: The Mesolens requires a custom microscope system with large scanning mirrors, specialized scan lens, and modified microscope stage due to its large physical dimensions.
evaluation: Claims C61-C69 describe the custom microscope system required for the Mesolens. These are factual descriptions of the instrument construction illustrated in Figure 1 and explained in Materials and methods.

result: Full Nyquist sampling with the Mesolens requires 20,000 x 20,000 pixels with 200 s acquisition time, comparable to stitched imaging with conventional objectives but without alignment problems.
evaluation: Claims C70-C76 present calculations of imaging requirements and comparisons with conventional approaches. The calculations are straightforward from the stated specifications and the comparison is reasonable.

result: Using electron-beam lithography test targets with 0.5, 1, and 2 µm gratings, the Mesolens achieved better than 1 µm lateral resolution in both brightfield and confocal modes.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88 describe resolution measurements using appropriate test targets (cited method from Oldenbourg et al., 1993) with results shown in Figure 2. The 1 µm grating was resolved while 0.5 µm was not, supporting the >1 µm resolution claim.

result: PSF measurements using fluorescent beads showed the Mesolens achieved 0.7-0.8 µm lateral and 7-8 µm axial resolution, close to theoretical values and far superior to conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. objectives.
evaluation: Claims C89-C98 present PSF measurements in Table 1 comparing Mesolens to conventional objectives. The measured values are close to theoretical predictions and demonstrate substantial improvement over conventional low-magnification objectives (38-51 µm vs 7-8 µm axial resolution).

result: The Mesolens' axial resolution in confocal mode (8 µm) was limited by aberrations in the scan lens rather than the objective itself, as evidenced by better performance (7 µm) in wide-field epi-fluorescence mode.
evaluation: Claims C99, C100, C102, C103, and C104 present the authors' interpretation of performance limitations based on comparison of confocal vs wide-field measurements in Table 1. The interpretation is reasonable given that wide-field performance is closer to theoretical limits.

result: Despite not achieving theoretical diffraction-limited axial resolution, the Mesolens z-resolution is sufficient for sub-cellular imaging and field flatness (≤3 µm over 4.2 mm) meets design specifications.
evaluation: Claims C101 and C105 are supported by the measured performance data in Table 1 and subsequent biological imaging results in Figures 4-5 showing individual cell nuclei throughout thick specimens.

result: The Mesolens demonstrated 25x higher light collection intensity compared to a conventional 4x/0.1 N.A. objective, consistent with its 4.7x higher numerical aperture.
evaluation: Claims C106-C108 and C116 describe throughput measurements using an LED standard. The 25x improvement is consistent with the expected relationship between N.A. and light collection (approximately N.A.²), supporting the measurement validity.

result: The complete Mesolens system has 11% on-axis transmission at 488 nm, comparable to commercial confocal microscopes when considering the entire optical path rather than just the objective.
evaluation: Claims C109-C115 present transmission measurements and comparisons. The authors provide reasonable explanations for losses and make fair comparisons to complete commercial systems rather than isolated objectives.

result: Wide-field epi-fluorescence imaging of triple-labeled rat brain explants demonstrated excellent chromatic correction with all three colors (DAPI, Alexa 488, Alexa 546) simultaneously in focus across the full field.
evaluation: Claims C117-C122 describe the multi-color imaging demonstration in Figure 3 and Video 1. The simultaneous focus of three wavelengths across the field directly demonstrates the chromatic correction claimed in the design specifications.

result: Direct comparison of the same 10-day mouse embryo imaged with Mesolens vs conventional 5x/0.15 N.A. objective showed the Mesolens resolved individual nuclei throughout the 2 mm thick specimen while the conventional objective showed poor z-resolution.
evaluation: Claims C123-C130 describe the comparative imaging experiment shown in Figure 4. The side-by-side comparison clearly demonstrates superior axial resolution with the Mesolens, with individual nuclei visible throughout depth vs needle-like artifacts with the conventional objective.

result: Anatomical structures in embryos were identified using standard references, signal remained constant with depth due to good specimen clearing, and no adjustments to laser power or gain were made during depth scanning.
evaluation: Claims C131-C133 describe methodology and observations. The citation to Kaufman 1992 for anatomical identification is appropriate, and the constant signal observation is consistent with well-cleared specimens.

result: Dual-color imaging of 12.5-day embryos with anti-beta-tubulin and acridine orange revealed fine anatomical details including heart muscle fibers, corneal endothelium, and eye structures throughout the specimen with maintained axial resolution across the full field.
evaluation: Claims C134-C142 describe the imaging of 12.5-day embryos shown in Figure 5, Video 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The images clearly show the claimed anatomical structures with sub-cellular detail, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 demonstrates maintained resolution across the field.

result: The Mesolens enables imaging of objects up to 6 mm wide and 3 mm thick with depth resolution of a few microns, allowing sub-cellular detail including individual nuclei and muscle fibers to be resolved throughout large intact specimens.
evaluation: Claims C3, C5, C143, and C147 state the main capability of the Mesolens. This is comprehensively supported by the resolution measurements (Table 1), comparative imaging (Figure 4), and biological demonstrations (Figures 3, 5) showing individual cells throughout intact embryos.

result: The Mesolens departs from century-old design principles by providing lateral resolution too high for direct viewing but suitable for high-pixel cameras and confocal scanning, with axial resolution justifying hundreds of optical sections.
evaluation: Claims C144-C146 describe the design philosophy. The departure from traditional design is supported by the specifications and demonstrated performance, though the claim about century-old principles is somewhat general.

result: The Mesolens enables biologists to assess developmental defects at multiple scales (organ shape, cell shape/number, nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio) in intact embryos, which no existing microscope can do in a single image.
evaluation: Claims C148-C149 describe biological applications enabled by the demonstrated capabilities. The claim is reasonable given the demonstrated ability to image from whole embryo to individual cells, though the assertion that no other microscope can do this is somewhat strong.

result: The Mesolens allows switching between slow laser scanning and fast camera modes in the same focal plane, which is not possible with higher magnification objectives and is valuable for finding rare features and adjusting corrections.
evaluation: Claims C150-C152 describe a practical advantage of the system. The capability is demonstrated in the methods and the advantage over high-magnification objectives is based on their limited field of view.

result: A complete Mesolens dataset is approximately 200x larger than a 100x/1.4 N.A. lens dataset, generating 639 GB for full Nyquist sampling of the 6x6x3 mm volume, which current computers can handle.
evaluation: Claims C154-C156 present calculations of data volume. The calculations are straightforward from the specifications and the assertion about computer capability is reasonable for 2016 technology.

result: Reduced signal in the center of 12.5-day embryos might be partly due to difficulty with acridine orange stain penetration in thicker specimens.
evaluation: Claim C153 is speculation about staining limitations. While reasonable, this is not directly tested and represents an interpretation of observed signal variation rather than a demonstrated result.

result: The Mesolens may enable applications in neurobiology (if tissue transparency is solved), measurement of mitotic index in slowly-reproducing tissues, and imaging of weakly fluorescent specimens.
evaluation: Claims C157-C160 are speculations about future applications. While reasonable extrapolations from the demonstrated capabilities, these are not tested in the manuscript and represent potential rather than demonstrated results.

result: Compared to a recently described lens by Sofroniew et al. (N.A. 0.6, 5 mm field, 1 mm depth) restricted to narrow wavelength band and single-spot multiphoton imaging, the Mesolens offers broader wavelength correction and multiple imaging modes.
evaluation: Claims C161-C163 compare the Mesolens to another large-field objective. The comparison is supported by citations and the demonstrated multi-wavelength, multi-mode capabilities of the Mesolens.

result: The Mesolens represents the most radical change in microscope objective design in over a century and has potential to transform optical microscopy through sub-cellular resolution 3D imaging of large specimens.
evaluation: Claims C164-C165 make strong assertions about historical significance and transformative potential. While the technical achievements are well-demonstrated, the claims about being the most radical change in a century and transforming the field are subjective assessments of impact rather than demonstrated results.

result: Alternative approaches including tissue expansion, camera lenses, photolithography lenses, FPM, Talbot microscopy, two-photon microscopy, serial sectioning, and commercial multizoom microscopes all have limitations preventing sub-cellular 3D imaging of large intact specimens.
evaluation: Claims C12-C42 review limitations of alternative approaches through citations to relevant literature. These claims establish the context and need for the Mesolens by documenting limitations of existing methods, supported by appropriate citations.
